items.title: Emergence & Context of Jainism
items.body:
## Why Jainism Arose (6th century BCE)

**In one line:** Jainism is an ancient Indian religion of extreme non-violence and self-discipline, systematised by Mahavira, the 24th and last Tirthankara (Tirthankara = a "ford-maker", a liberated teacher who shows the way across the ocean of rebirth).

**Why it is asked:** Jainism rose in the same 6th-century-BCE protest against Vedic ritualism as Buddhism, so examiners test its founders, vows, sects and councils and often make you tell it apart from Buddhism.

**The story**

Jainism emerged in the **6th century BCE** as a reaction to the growing **complexity, ritualism and hierarchy** of the **Vedic religion**.

- **Religious unrest:** Vedic worship centred on **sacrifices, mantras and rituals** that were **expensive and inaccessible** to the common people.
- **Brahmin dominance:** Brahmins positioned themselves as the **highest caste** and demanded privileges, causing social division and unrest.
- **Kshatriya & Vaishya opposition:** these classes reacted against **Brahmin domination**; the search for an **egalitarian path** gave rise to Jainism (and Buddhism).
- **Appeal of Jainism:** it offered **equality**, relief from the **Varna system**, and **simple teachings in Prakrit** (the people's language), stressing **Ahimsa (non-violence)** and self-discipline.

**TL;DR**

- Jainism emerged in the 6th century BCE against Vedic ritualism and Brahmin supremacy.
- Vedic sacrifices/mantras were costly and inaccessible to the common people.
- Kshatriyas and Vaishyas opposed Brahmin domination, seeking an egalitarian path.
- Jainism offered equality and relief from the Varna system.
- Mahavira taught in Prakrit, stressing Ahimsa and self-discipline, aiding its spread.

Jainism offered equality and relief from the Varna system.
Mahavira taught in Prakrit, stressing Ahimsa and self-discipline, aiding its spread.

items.title: The 24 Tirthankaras
items.body:
## Spiritual Ford-Makers

**In one line** — Jainism recognises 24 Tirthankaras (enlightened ford-makers) as role models.

**The story**

Jainism traces its roots through **24 Tirthankaras** — spiritual leaders who attained enlightenment and serve as role models.

- **Rishabhanatha (Adinath)** — the **1st Tirthankara**; symbol **Bull**; said to have established the **Ikshvaku dynasty** and laid the foundation of Jain teachings.
- **Parshvanatha** — the **23rd Tirthankara**; symbol **Snake (serpent)**; preached a simpler four-fold Jainism before Mahavira and believed in the **eternity of matter**.
- **Mahavira** — the **24th and last Tirthankara**; symbol **Lion**; gave Jainism its current structured form.
- Each Tirthankara has a distinctive **symbol** (e.g. Rishabhanatha–Bull, Ajitanatha–Elephant, Neminatha–Conch, Parshvanatha–Snake, Mahavira–Lion).
- **Mallinatha (19th)** is traditionally regarded (in the Svetambara view) as the **only female Tirthankara**.

**TL;DR**

- Jainism recognises 24 Tirthankaras (enlightened ford-makers) as role models.
- Rishabhanatha (Adinath) — 1st Tirthankara, symbol Bull, linked to the Ikshvaku dynasty.
- Parshvanatha — 23rd Tirthankara, symbol Snake, believed in the eternity of matter.
- Mahavira — 24th and last Tirthankara, symbol Lion, gave Jainism its present form.
- Mallinatha (19th) is regarded as the only female Tirthankara.

items.title: Vardhamana Mahavira — Life
items.body:
## The 24th Tirthankara

**In one line** — Mahavira: 24th Tirthankara, born 540 BCE at Kundagrama near Vaishali, Bihar.

**The story**

- **Birth:** born in **540 BCE** at **Kundagrama**, near **Vaishali**, in modern-day **Bihar**.
- **Parents:** father **Siddhartha** was head of the **Jnatrika clan**; mother **Trishala** was a **Lichchavi princess**.
- **Family:** married **Yashoda**; had a daughter named **Anojja**.
- **Renunciation:** at the age of **30** he renounced worldly life and became an ascetic.
- **Enlightenment:** after **12 years** of severe austerities he attained **Kevala Jnana (Supreme Knowledge)** at the age of **42**.
- **Preaching:** spent **30 years** spreading Jainism across northern India, especially **Kosala, Magadha and Mithila**.
- **Death (Nirvana):** died at the age of **72** in **468 BCE** at **Pavapuri, Bihar**.

## Don't confuse
- **Yashoda vs Yashodhara:** **Yashoda** was Mahavira's *wife*; **Yashodhara** was the *Buddha's* wife — exams swap these deliberately.
- **Four vows vs five vows:** **Parshvanatha** (23rd Tirthankara) taught **four** vows; **Mahavira** added the fifth (Brahmacharya, celibacy) to make the **five** great vows (Pancha Mahavrata).
- **Trishala (mother) vs Siddhartha (father):** Mahavira's mother was **Trishala** (Lichchhavi clan); his father was **Siddhartha** of the Jnatrika clan — unrelated to Buddha's father, also named Suddhodana.

**TL;DR**

- Mahavira: 24th Tirthankara, born 540 BCE at Kundagrama near Vaishali, Bihar.
- Father Siddhartha (Jnatrika clan chief); mother Trishala (Lichchavi princess).
- Married Yashoda; daughter Anojja; renounced worldly life at age 30.
- Attained Kevala Jnana at 42 after 12 years of austerities.
- Died at 72 in 468 BCE at Pavapuri, Bihar.
- Mahavira attained nirvana (death) at Pawapuri (Pava), near Rajgir, c. 527/468 BCE.

items.title: Parshvanatha & the Four Vows
items.body:
## The 23rd Tirthankara's Teaching

**In one line** — Parshvanatha (23rd Tirthankara) taught a simpler Jainism before Mahavira.

**The story**

**Parshvanatha**, the **23rd Tirthankara**, preached a **simple form of Jainism** before Mahavira.

- He advocated **four doctrines (four vows)**, which **Mahavira later expanded to five**.
- Parshvanatha's followers practised:
  - **Non-violence** (Ahimsa)
  - **Truth** (Satya)
  - **Non-stealing** (Asteya)
  - **Renunciation / non-attachment** (Aparigraha)
- Mahavira **added celibacy (Brahmacharya)** as the **fifth vow**.
- Parshvanatha is associated with the **Snake** symbol and believed in the **eternity of matter**.

**TL;DR**

- Parshvanatha (23rd Tirthankara) taught a simpler Jainism before Mahavira.
- He advocated four vows: non-violence, truth, non-stealing, non-attachment.
- Mahavira later expanded these four into five vows.
- The fifth vow added by Mahavira was Brahmacharya (celibacy).
- Parshvanatha's symbol is the Snake; he believed in the eternity of matter.
keyPoints: Parshvanatha (23rd Tirthankara) taught a simpler Jainism before Mahavira.
He advocated four vows: non-violence, truth, non-stealing, non-attachment.
Mahavira later expanded these four into five vows.
The fifth vow added by Mahavira was Brahmacharya (celibacy).
Parshvanatha's symbol is the Snake; he believed in the eternity of matter.

items.title: Five Vows — Pancha Mahavrata
items.body:
## The Five Great Vows

**In one line** — Pancha Mahavrata = five great vows for ascetics and householders.

**The story**

Mahavira expanded the earlier teachings into **five key doctrines (Pancha Mahavratas)** for ascetics and householders:

| Vow | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Ahimsa** | Non-violence toward all living beings; complete avoidance of harm |
| **Satya** | Always speak the truth; lies are harmful and unethical |
| **Asteya** | Do not steal or take what is not freely given |
| **Aparigraha** | Renounce possessions; practise non-attachment |
| **Brahmacharya** | Practise celibacy/chastity (added by Mahavira to Parshvanatha's four) |

- For **householders**, Mahavira prescribed a **simplified version** of these vows called **Anuvratas** (lesser vows), avoiding the strict renunciation required of monks.

**TL;DR**

- Pancha Mahavrata = five great vows for ascetics and householders.
- Ahimsa (non-violence), Satya (truth), Asteya (non-stealing).
- Aparigraha (non-attachment) and Brahmacharya (celibacy).
- Brahmacharya was the fifth vow added by Mahavira to Parshvanatha's four.
- Householders follow a simplified version called Anuvratas (lesser vows).

items.title: Three Jewels — Ratnatraya (Triratna)
items.body:
## The Path to Liberation

**In one line** — Three Jewels (Ratnatraya/Triratna) form the Jain path to liberation.

**The story**

The path to **Moksha** in Jainism rests on **three essential principles** — the **Three Jewels (Ratnatraya / Triratna)**:

| Jewel | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Samyak Darshan** | Right faith — rejection of superstition, acceptance of truth |
| **Samyak Gyan** | Right knowledge — understanding reality without false perception |
| **Samyak Charitra** | Right conduct — ethical behaviour in every aspect of life |

- Together these lead to the **removal of karma** and **purification of the soul**, achieving **Moksha/Nirvana** — liberation from the cycle of birth, pain and death.
- The Triratna remains relevant today for stressing **moral integrity, equality and self-discipline**.

**TL;DR**

- Three Jewels (Ratnatraya/Triratna) form the Jain path to liberation.
- Samyak Darshan = Right Faith (rejecting superstition, accepting truth).
- Samyak Gyan = Right Knowledge (reality without false perception).
- Samyak Charitra = Right Conduct (ethical behaviour in all life).
- Together they remove karma and purify the soul, leading to Moksha/Nirvana.
keyPoints: Three Jewels (Ratnatraya/Triratna) form the Jain path to liberation.
Samyak Darshan = Right Faith (rejecting superstition, accepting truth).
Samyak Gyan = Right Knowledge (reality without false perception).
Samyak Charitra = Right Conduct (ethical behaviour in all life).
Together they remove karma and purify the soul, leading to Moksha/Nirvana.

items.title: Anekantavada & Syadvada
items.body:
## Doctrines of Many-Sidedness

**In one line** — Anekantavada = non-absolutism: reality understood only through multiple perspectives.

**The story**

Jain epistemology stresses that reality is **complex and multifaceted**:

- **Anekantavada (Non-absolutism):** reality is complex and can be fully understood only by considering **multiple perspectives**; **absolute truth is beyond human comprehension**, so one must stay open to other viewpoints.
- **Syadvada (theory of 'maybe'):** all judgments are **conditional** and true only under **certain conditions**. The word **'Syat'** means **'maybe'**, indicating reality is **multifaceted**; it promotes **intellectual flexibility**.
- Together they teach **intellectual and social tolerance**, valued today for accommodating **diverse perspectives**.

**TL;DR**

- Anekantavada = non-absolutism: reality understood only through multiple perspectives.
- It holds absolute truth is beyond full human comprehension.
- Syadvada = theory of conditional judgments; 'Syat' means 'maybe'.
- Syadvada promotes intellectual flexibility and many-sided reality.
- Both foster intellectual and social tolerance.
keyPoints: Anekantavada = non-absolutism: reality understood only through multiple perspectives.
It holds absolute truth is beyond full human comprehension.
Syadvada = theory of conditional judgments; 'Syat' means 'maybe'.
Syadvada promotes intellectual flexibility and many-sided reality.
Both foster intellectual and social tolerance.
items.mnemonic: "Syat = maybe" (Syadvada, conditional judgments); "Aneka = many" (Anekantavada, many viewpoints).

items.title: Soul, Matter & the Five Types of Knowledge
items.body:
## Jiva, Ajiva and Jnana

**In one line** — Universe = Jiva (soul) + Ajiva (matter); the soul accumulates karma.

**The story**

Mahavira taught that the universe consists of **two fundamental entities**:

- **Jiva (soul):** the conscious, living entity that **accumulates karma** through desires and actions.
- **Ajiva (matter):** the **non-living** elements. In Jainism **all beings have a soul** — even inanimate objects — which can experience suffering.

### Five Types of Knowledge (Jnana)

| Knowledge | Nature |
|---|---|
| **Mati Jnana** | Through the senses and mind |
| **Sruta Jnana** | From scriptures and teachings |
| **Avadhi Jnana** | Clairvoyant knowledge of distant objects/events |
| **Manahparyaya Jnana** | Telepathic — knowing others' thoughts |
| **Kevala Jnana** | The highest — omniscience through enlightenment |

**TL;DR**

- Universe = Jiva (soul) + Ajiva (matter); the soul accumulates karma.
- All beings, even inanimate objects, have a soul that can suffer.
- Five knowledges: Mati (senses/mind), Sruta (scriptures).
- Avadhi (clairvoyance) and Manahparyaya (telepathy).
- Kevala Jnana = highest, omniscience attained through enlightenment.

items.title: Sects — Digambara & Svetambara
items.body:
## The Two Great Sects

**In one line** — Digambara = 'sky-clad' (nudity); Svetambara = 'white-clad'.

**The story**

| Aspect | **Digambara** | **Svetambara** |
|---|---|---|
| **Meaning** | Sky-clad (nudity as renunciation) | White-clad (wear white clothing) |
| **Women & liberation** | Women cannot attain liberation without rebirth as a man | Women can attain liberation |
| **Idols** | Nude, eyes downcast | Adorned, eyes open, often jewelled |
| **Founder/leader** | **Bhadrabahu** led the migration during the 12-year famine | **Sthulbhadra** led the sect that stayed in Magadha |
| **Practices** | Strict asceticism, nudity for monks | Monks wear white, more relaxed ascetic code |
| **Canon** | Hold that the original Agamas were lost | Preserve the canonical texts (**Agamas**), composed in **Ardhamagadhi Prakrit** |

- **Background:** both sects look back to **Mahavira**, who attained **nirvana (death) at Pawapuri** (Bihar); the split came later, after Bhadrabahu's famine migration to the south.
- **Digambara sub-sects:** Mula Sangh (Acharya Kundakunda), Bisapantha, Digambar Terapantha, Taranpantha.
- **Svetambara sub-sects:** Sthanakavasi, Murtipujaka (Deravasi), Terapanthi — Sthanakavasi and Terapanthi monks wear a **muhapatti** (mouth-cloth).

**TL;DR**

- Digambara = 'sky-clad' (nudity); Svetambara = 'white-clad'.
- Digambara: women need rebirth as a man for liberation; Svetambara: women can attain it.
- Digambara idols nude with eyes downcast; Svetambara idols adorned, eyes open.
- Bhadrabahu led the famine migration (Digambara); Sthulbhadra stayed in Magadha (Svetambara).
- Sthanakavasi & Terapanthi monks wear a muhapatti (mouth-cloth) and reject idols.
- Sthanakvasi — a Svetambara sub-sect that rejects idol/image worship (aniconic).

items.title: Jain Councils
items.body:
## Compilation of the Canon

**In one line** — First Jain Council: 300 BCE at Pataliputra, presided by Sthulbhadra.

**The story**

| Council | Year | Venue | Presided by | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **First Jain Council** | **300 BCE** | **Pataliputra** (Bihar) | **Sthulbhadra** | Compilation of the Jain canon into **12 Angas** |
| **Second Jain Council** | **512 CE** | **Vallabhi** (Gujarat) | **Devardhigani Kshemasarmana** | Expansion of the canon with **Upangas** and **final compilation** of scriptures |

- The **First Council** at Pataliputra organised the surviving teachings into the **twelve Angas**.
- The **Second Council** at Vallabhi produced the **final written compilation** of Jain scriptures.

**TL;DR**

- First Jain Council: 300 BCE at Pataliputra, presided by Sthulbhadra.
- First Council compiled the Jain canon into 12 Angas.
- Second Jain Council: 512 CE at Vallabhi (Gujarat).
- Second Council presided by Devardhigani Kshemasarmana.
- Second Council added Upangas and produced the final compilation of scriptures.

Second Council added Upangas and produced the final compilation of scriptures.

items.title: Jain Symbols
items.body:
## Sacred Symbols and Their Meaning

**In one line** — Swastika = peace and well-being; Nandavarta = spiritual advancement (9-endpoint swastika).

**The story**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Swastika** | Peace and well-being of all humans |
| **Nandavarta** | A large swastika with nine endpoints — spiritual advancement |
| **Bhadrasana** | A throne sanctified by the feet of Tirthankaras |
| **Shrivatsa** | A mark on the chest of Tirthankaras — the pure soul |
| **Darpana** | A mirror — self-reflection and discovery of the inner self |
| **Minayugala** | A pair of fish — conquest over sexual desires |
| **Vardhamanaka** | A shallow dish/lamp — increase in wealth, merit, prosperity |
| **Kalasha** | A pot of pure water — purity and well-being of all beings |

**TL;DR**

- Swastika = peace and well-being; Nandavarta = spiritual advancement (9-endpoint swastika).
- Bhadrasana = throne of Tirthankaras; Shrivatsa = pure soul mark on the chest.
- Darpana (mirror) = self-reflection; Minayugala (pair of fish) = conquest of desire.
- Vardhamanaka (dish/lamp) = increasing wealth and merit.
- Kalasha (pot of pure water) = purity and well-being of all beings.

items.title: Jain Literature — Agamas
items.body:
## Canonical & Non-Canonical Texts

**In one line** — Jain literature = Agam (canonical) and Non-Agam (secondary) texts.

**The story**

Jain literature falls into **two main categories**:

### Agam Literature (Canonical)
- Contains the **direct teachings of Lord Mahavir**, compiled by his followers.
- **Ang-agamas (main texts):** compiled by the **Ganadharas** (Mahavir's immediate disciples), who possessed **Keval-Gyan**; they compiled **twelve Ang-agamas**.
- **Ang-bahya-agamas (secondary texts):** expansions written by monks called **Shrutakevalins** (who knew at least ten Purvas).
- The **12th Ang-agama, Drastivad**, contains **fourteen Purva texts (Purva-agams)** — the **oldest sacred Jain texts**.
- **Language:** all Agam literature is in **Prakrit**.

### Non-Agam Literature
- **Commentaries and explanations** of the Agamas, plus independent works by elder monks, nuns and scholars.
- Written in many languages — **Prakrit, Sanskrit, Old Marathi, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Tamil, German and English**.

**TL;DR**

- Jain literature = Agam (canonical) and Non-Agam (secondary) texts.
- Ang-agamas: twelve main texts compiled by the Ganadharas (Mahavir's disciples).
- Ang-bahya-agamas: expansions written by Shrutakevalins (knew ≥10 Purvas).
- The 12th Anga (Drastivad) holds the 14 Purvas — oldest sacred Jain texts.
- All Agam literature is in Prakrit; Non-Agam works span many languages.
- The Jain canonical texts (Agamas/Angas) were composed in Ardhamagadhi Prakrit.
keyPoints: Jain literature = Agam (canonical) and Non-Agam (secondary) texts.
Ang-agamas: twelve main texts compiled by the Ganadharas (Mahavir's disciples).
Ang-bahya-agamas: expansions written by Shrutakevalins (knew ≥10 Purvas).
The 12th Anga (Drastivad) holds the 14 Purvas — oldest sacred Jain texts.

The Jain canonical texts (Agamas/Angas) were composed in Ardhamagadhi Prakrit.

items.title: Jain Architecture
items.body:
## Caves, Statues & Temples

**In one line** — Caves: Ellora (30–35), Mangi-Tungi, Gajapantha (Maharashtra); Udayagiri-Khandagiri, Hathi-gumpha (Odisha); Sittanavasal (Tamil Nadu).

**The story**

Jain architecture, though influenced by Hindu and Buddhist styles, developed unique features.

### Caves (Layana / Gumphas)
- Rock-cut caves where monks lived: **Ellora (Caves 30–35)**, **Mangi-Tungi** and **Gajapantha** (Maharashtra); **Udayagiri-Khandagiri** and **Hathi-gumpha** (Odisha); **Sittanavasal** (Tamil Nadu).

### Statues
- **Gomateshwara / Bahubali statue, Shravanabelagola (Karnataka)** — one of the tallest **monolithic** statues in the world.
- **Statue of Ahimsa (Rishabnatha), Mangi-Tungi hills (Maharashtra)**.

### Temples (Jinalayas / Basadis)
- **Dilwara Temple, Mount Abu (Rajasthan)** — renowned for intricate marble carvings.
- **Girnar and Palitana temples (Gujarat)**; **Muktagiri (Maharashtra)**.

### Features
- **Manastambha:** an ornamental pillar with a Tirthankara image on all four cardinal directions, in front of temples.
- **Basadis:** Jain monastic establishments, prominent in **Karnataka**.

**TL;DR**

- Caves: Ellora (30–35), Mangi-Tungi, Gajapantha (Maharashtra); Udayagiri-Khandagiri, Hathi-gumpha (Odisha); Sittanavasal (Tamil Nadu).
- Gomateshwara/Bahubali at Shravanabelagola (Karnataka) — among the tallest monolithic statues.
- Dilwara Temple, Mount Abu — famed for intricate marble carvings.
- Manastambha: pillar with a Tirthankara image on all four cardinal directions.
- Basadis: Jain monastic establishments, prominent in Karnataka.

items.title: Spread of Jainism & Royal Patronage
items.body:
## How Jainism Spread

**In one line** — Mahavira had eleven Ganadharas (heads of schools).

**The story**

- **Mahavira's travels:** he preached extensively; his **simple life, penance and austerity** attracted many followers.
- **Ganadharas:** Mahavira had **eleven disciples (Ganadharas)**, heads of schools. After his death, **Arya Sudharma** was the **only surviving Ganadhara** and became the **first Thera** (chief preceptor) of the Jain order.
- **Jain monks:** spread the faith through **scholarly discussion** and personal simplicity.
- **Royal patronage:**
  - **Udayin**, successor of **Ajatasatru**, was a devoted Jaina.
  - **Chandragupta Maurya**, a follower, migrated with **Bhadrabahu** to **South India**, spreading Jainism in the south.
  - **Mathura and Ujjain** became major centres of Jainism in the early Christian centuries.
  - Theras **Sambhutavijaya and Bhadrabahu** were prominent during the **Nanda dynasty**.

**TL;DR**

- Mahavira had eleven Ganadharas (heads of schools).
- Arya Sudharma, the only surviving Ganadhara, became the first Thera of the order.
- Udayin, successor of Ajatasatru, was a devoted Jaina.
- Chandragupta Maurya migrated with Bhadrabahu to South India, spreading Jainism.
- Mathura and Ujjain emerged as major Jain centres in the early Christian era.
keyPoints: Mahavira had eleven Ganadharas (heads of schools).
Arya Sudharma, the only surviving Ganadhara, became the first Thera of the order.
Udayin, successor of Ajatasatru, was a devoted Jaina.
Chandragupta Maurya migrated with Bhadrabahu to South India, spreading Jainism.
Mathura and Ujjain emerged as major Jain centres in the early Christian era.

items.title: All 24 Tirthankaras — Symbols & Birthplaces
items.body:
## The full list of 24 Tirthankaras

**In one line:** each of the 24 Tirthankaras (ford-makers) has a fixed number, a birthplace and a symbol (lanchhana) used to identify his image.

**Why it is asked:** examiners pair a Tirthankara with his symbol or number (Rishabhanatha–Bull, Neminatha–Conch, Parshvanatha–Snake, Mahavira–Lion) and test "only/first/last" facts.

**The story**

| No. | Tirthankara | Birthplace | Symbol |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1st | Rishabhanatha (Adinath) | Ayodhya | Bull |
| 2nd | Ajitanatha | Ayodhya | Elephant |
| 3rd | Sambhavanatha | Sravasti | Horse |
| 4th | Abhinandananatha | Ayodhya | Ape |
| 5th | Sumatinatha | Ayodhya | Heron |
| 6th | Padmaprabha | Kausambi | Lotus |
| 7th | Suparshvanatha | Varanasi | Swastika |
| 8th | Chandraprabha | Chandrapuri | Moon |
| 9th | Suvidhinatha (Pushpadanta) | Kakandi | Dolphin (sea dragon) |
| 10th | Shitalanatha | Bhadrikapuri | Shrivatsa |
| 11th | Shreyansanatha | Simhapuri | Rhinoceros |
| 12th | Vasupujya | Champapuri | Buffalo |
| 13th | Vimalanatha | Kampilya | Boar |
| 14th | Anantanatha | Ayodhya | Hawk (or Bear) |
| 15th | Dharmanatha | Ratnapuri | Thunderbolt |
| 16th | Shantinatha | Hastinapur | Deer |
| 17th | Kunthunatha | Hastinapur | Goat |
| 18th | Aranatha | Hastinapur | Fish (or Nandyavarta) |
| 19th | Mallinatha | Mithila | Water Pot |
| 20th | Munisuvrata | Rajagriha | Tortoise |
| 21st | Naminatha | Mithila | Blue Lotus |
| 22nd | Neminatha (Arishtanemi) | Sauripur | Conch Shell |
| 23rd | Parshvanatha | Varanasi | Snake |
| 24th | Mahavira | Kundagrama (Vaishali) | Lion |

**Remember it:** five were born at **Ayodhya** (1st, 2nd, 4th, 5th, 14th); three at **Hastinapur** (16th–18th); two at **Mithila** (19th, 21st); two at **Varanasi** (7th, 23rd).

## Don't confuse
- **Shrivatsa** is both the symbol of the 10th Tirthankara (Shitalanatha) and one of the eight auspicious Jain symbols (a mark on the chest).
- **Lotus** = 6th Padmaprabha; **Blue Lotus** = 21st Naminatha.
- **Swastika** = 7th Suparshvanatha's symbol; **Snake** = 23rd Parshvanatha (the names sound alike).

**TL;DR**
- 1st Rishabhanatha–Bull (Ayodhya); 22nd Neminatha–Conch Shell (Sauripur); 23rd Parshvanatha–Snake (Varanasi); 24th Mahavira–Lion (Kundagrama).
- 19th Mallinatha (Mithila, Water Pot) is the only female Tirthankara.
keyPoints: 1st Rishabhanatha–Bull–Ayodhya; 2nd Ajitanatha–Elephant–Ayodhya.
16th Shantinatha–Deer, 17th Kunthunatha–Goat, 18th Aranatha–Fish: all born at Hastinapur.
19th Mallinatha–Water Pot–Mithila; 20th Munisuvrata–Tortoise–Rajagriha; 21st Naminatha–Blue Lotus–Mithila.
22nd Neminatha (Arishtanemi)–Conch Shell–Sauripur.
23rd Parshvanatha–Snake–Varanasi; 24th Mahavira–Lion–Kundagrama (Vaishali).

items.title: Mahavira & Parshvanatha — Titles, Kaivalya Site, Companions
items.body:
## More about the last two Tirthankaras

**In one line:** beyond the dates, exams ask Mahavira's titles, where he attained Kaivalya, who his companions were, and where Parshvanatha came from.

**Why it is asked:** these are classic "who/where" one-liners and Buddha-vs-Mahavira traps.

**The story**

### Mahavira
| Point | Fact |
|---|---|
| Titles | **Jina** (the conqueror — his followers are called **Jainas**), **Mahavira** (great hero), **Nirgrantha / Nigrantha** (free from bonds), **Kevalin** (the omniscient one) |
| Kaivalya | Attained Kevala Jnana (also called **Kaivalya**) under a **sal tree** at **Jrimbhikagrama** on the bank of the river **Rijupalika** |
| Other dates | Traditional Jain dates: born **599 BCE**, died **527 BCE** (historians often use 540–468 BCE) |
| Family | Mother **Trishala** was the sister of **Chetaka**, the Lichchhavi chief of Vaishali; elder brother **Nandivardhana** |
| First disciple | **Indrabhuti Gautama** was the first of the eleven Ganadharas |
| Son-in-law | **Jamali**, husband of his daughter, led the **first schism** in the order |
| Companion | **Makkhali Gosala** lived with Mahavira for about **six years**, then founded the **Ajivika** sect |
| Language | He preached in **Ardhamagadhi**, a Prakrit language |

### Parshvanatha
- Son of King **Ashvasena** of **Varanasi (Kashi)**; lived about **250 years before Mahavira** (c. 8th century BCE) — the earliest Tirthankara accepted as historical.
- Attained nirvana at **Sammed Shikhar** (Parasnath hill, Jharkhand).

## Don't confuse
- Mahavira's father was named **Siddhartha** — the same as the Buddha's personal name (Siddhartha Gautama). The Buddha's father was **Suddhodana**.
- **Kevala Jnana / Kaivalya** (omniscience, at 42) is different from **nirvana** (death at Pavapuri, at 72).

**TL;DR**
- Jina = conqueror; Nirgrantha = free from bonds; Kevalin = omniscient.
- Kaivalya under a sal tree, Jrimbhikagrama, river Rijupalika.
- Gosala (Ajivika founder) and Jamali (first schism) were Mahavira's associates.
keyPoints: Jina means 'conqueror'; Mahavira was also called Nirgrantha (free from bonds) and Kevalin.
Kaivalya: under a sal tree at Jrimbhikagrama on the river Rijupalika.
Traditional Jain dates for Mahavira: 599–527 BCE.
Makkhali Gosala, founder of the Ajivikas, was with Mahavira for six years; Jamali led the first schism.
Parshvanatha: son of King Ashvasena of Varanasi; nirvana at Sammed Shikhar.

items.title: Jain Texts & Doctrine — Exam Extras
items.body:
## Texts and beliefs that previous papers test

**In one line:** besides the Agamas, exams ask which texts are Jain, what Jains believe about God, soul and karma, and how Jain ethics shaped Jain society.

**Why it is asked:** UPSC 2022 asked which texts are Jaina; UPSC 2013 asked Jain doctrine on soul and karma; UPSC 2018 asked Sthanakvasi.

**The story**

### Jain texts (name → what it is)
| Text | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Acharanga Sutra** | First of the 12 Angas — rules of conduct for Jain monks |
| **Bhagavati Sutra** | An Anga that gives a list of the **16 Mahajanapadas** |
| **Kalpasutra** | Lives of the Tirthankaras; traditionally ascribed to **Bhadrabahu** |
| **Parishishtaparvan** | Written by **Hemachandra** (12th century); tells of Chandragupta Maurya's conversion |
| **Trishashti-lakshana Mahapurana** | Digambara text by **Jinasena** and Gunabhadra on the 63 great men |
| **Upangas** | The 12 secondary canonical texts added to the 12 Angas |

- **Trap:** Nettipakarana and Avadanashataka are **Buddhist** texts, not Jain.

### Doctrine
- **No creator God:** Jainism recognises gods but places them **below the Jina**; the universe is eternal.
- **Soul everywhere:** every object, even the **smallest particle**, has a soul (jiva).
- **Karma is the bane of the soul:** it binds the soul; **penance (austerity) destroys karma**.
- **Sallekhana:** voluntary fasting unto death, the ideal Jain end.
- **Varna:** Jainism did **not condemn the varna system** as sharply as Buddhism did; birth in a higher or lower varna was explained by past karma.
- **Ahimsa and work:** farming harms insects, so Jains took to **trade and commerce**.
- **Today:** **Aparigraha** (non-attachment) is cited as a check on **consumerism** and greed; Jain Ahimsa shaped Gandhi.

**TL;DR**
- Acharanga = first Anga; Bhagavati = 16 Mahajanapadas; Kalpasutra = Bhadrabahu; Parishishtaparvan = Hemachandra.
- No creator God; every particle has a soul; penance destroys karma; Sallekhana = fast unto death.
keyPoints: Acharanga Sutra is the first Anga (conduct of monks); the Bhagavati Sutra lists 16 Mahajanapadas.
Kalpasutra is ascribed to Bhadrabahu; Parishishtaparvan is by Hemachandra.
Trishashti-lakshana Mahapurana (Jinasena) is a Jaina text; Nettipakarana and Avadanashataka are Buddhist.
Jainism: no creator God (gods rank below the Jina); every particle has a soul; penance destroys karma.
Sallekhana = voluntary fast unto death; Ahimsa pushed Jains from farming into trade.

items.title: Jain Sites, Patrons & the AP Angle
items.body:
## Where Jainism flourished and who supported it

**In one line:** Jain holy sites and royal patrons are tested as place–state and king–religion pairs.

**Why it is asked:** pairs like Shravanabelagola–Karnataka, Dilwara–Rajasthan, Hathigumpha–Kharavela and Sammed Shikhar–Jharkhand recur; AP papers add local sites.

**The story**

### Sites
| Site | State | Why famous |
|---|---|---|
| **Sammed Shikhar** (Parasnath hill) | Jharkhand | **20 of the 24 Tirthankaras** attained nirvana here |
| **Shravanabelagola** | Karnataka | 57-ft (about 17 m) **Gomateshwara** monolith on Vindhyagiri hill, made c. **981 CE** for **Chamundaraya**, minister of the **Western Ganga** king; **Mahamastakabhisheka** every **12 years**; **Chandragupta Maurya** died by Sallekhana on **Chandragiri** hill |
| **Dilwara** (Mount Abu) | Rajasthan | Vimal Vasahi temple built in **1031 CE** by **Vimal Shah**, minister of the Solanki (Chalukya) king Bhima I; Luna Vasahi by **Vastupala–Tejapala** |
| **Ranakpur** | Rajasthan | Adinath temple famed for its **1,444 carved pillars** |
| **Palitana** (Shatrunjaya hills) | Gujarat | Hill covered with hundreds of Jain temples |
| **Girnar** (Junagadh) | Gujarat | Linked with the 22nd Tirthankara **Neminatha** |
| **Udayagiri–Khandagiri** | Odisha | Caves near Bhubaneswar cut for Jain monks; **Hathigumpha inscription** of **Kharavela** of Kalinga |
| **Sittanavasal** | Tamil Nadu | Jain cave with **paintings** (Pudukkottai) |
| **Kankali Tila** | Uttar Pradesh | Jain stupa and sculptures at **Mathura** |
| **Mangi-Tungi** | Maharashtra | 108-ft **Statue of Ahimsa** of Rishabhanatha (2016) |

### Royal patrons
- **Kharavela** (Kalinga, 1st century BCE) — Jain king, Hathigumpha inscription.
- **Chandragupta Maurya** — went south with Bhadrabahu; Sallekhana at Shravanabelagola.
- **Kumarapala** (Solanki/Chalukya of Gujarat) — guided by **Hemachandra**.
- **Amoghavarsha I** (Rashtrakuta), the **Western Gangas** and the Kadambas — patrons in the Deccan and south.

### AP angle
- **Danavulapadu** (YSR Kadapa district) — Jain site with Rashtrakuta-period Jain remains.
- **Ramatheertham** (Vizianagaram) — hill with both **Jain and Buddhist** remains.
- **Kolanupaka** — famous Jain temple, now in **Telangana** (not Andhra Pradesh).

**TL;DR**
- Sammed Shikhar (Jharkhand) = nirvana of 20 Tirthankaras.
- Gomateshwara: Chamundaraya, Western Ganga, c. 981 CE, Mahamastakabhisheka every 12 years.
- Dilwara (Vimal Shah, 1031 CE); Hathigumpha (Kharavela); Danavulapadu and Ramatheertham (AP).
keyPoints: Sammed Shikhar (Parasnath hill, Jharkhand): 20 of the 24 Tirthankaras attained nirvana there.
Gomateshwara (57 ft) at Shravanabelagola was made c. 981 CE for Chamundaraya, a Western Ganga minister; Mahamastakabhisheka every 12 years.
Dilwara Vimal Vasahi: built 1031 CE by Vimal Shah; Ranakpur has 1,444 pillars.
Kharavela of Kalinga — Hathigumpha inscription; Kumarapala — Hemachandra; Amoghavarsha I — Rashtrakuta patron.
AP: Danavulapadu (YSR Kadapa) and Ramatheertham (Vizianagaram); Kolanupaka is in Telangana.

items.title: Jain Sub-sects — Digambara & Svetambara Branches
items.body:
## The branches inside each sect

**In one line:** each of the two great sects split further, mostly over idol worship and the role of Bhattarakas (resident dharma gurus).

**Why it is asked:** "Sthanakvasi belongs to which religion?" (UPSC 2018) and sub-sect–feature matching.

**The story**

### Digambara sub-sects
| Sub-sect | Feature |
|---|---|
| **Mula Sangh** | Associated with **Acharya Kundakunda**; known from **430 AD**; branches **Nandi Gana, Sena Gana, Deva Gana, Simha Gana** |
| **Bisapantha** | Worship Tirthankaras, **Yakshas and Yakshinis** with aarti, flowers, fruits and prasad; accept **Bhattarakas** as dharma gurus; mainly Rajasthan and Gujarat |
| **Digambar Terapantha** | Worship idols with ashtadravya but use **dry** substitutes for flowers and fruits; reject Bhattarakas; worship only Tirthankaras |
| **Taranpantha** | Refute idolatry; temples keep sacred **books** for worship; stress study of scripture |

### Svetambara sub-sects
| Sub-sect | Feature |
|---|---|
| **Sthanakavasi** | Pray to saints, not idols; saints wear a **muhapatti** (mouth-cloth) |
| **Murtipujaka (Deravasi)** | Keep and worship idols in temples; saints do **not** wear a muhapatti |
| **Terapanthi** | Like Sthanakavasi — pray to saints, wear a muhapatti |

## Don't confuse
- **Terapantha** (Digambara, dry offerings) vs **Terapanthi** (Svetambara, muhapatti, no idols).
- **Murtipujaka** = idol worshippers; **Sthanakavasi** and **Taranpantha** reject idols.

**TL;DR**
- Digambara: Mula Sangh (Kundakunda), Bisapantha (Bhattarakas), Terapantha (dry offerings), Taranpantha (books).
- Svetambara: Sthanakavasi and Terapanthi (muhapatti, no idols), Murtipujaka (idols).
keyPoints: Mula Sangh (Digambara) — Acharya Kundakunda, from 430 AD; Nandi, Sena, Deva and Simha Ganas.
Bisapantha accept Bhattarakas as dharma gurus; Digambar Terapantha reject them and use dry offerings.
Taranpantha refute idolatry and worship sacred books.
Svetambara: Sthanakavasi and Terapanthi wear the muhapatti; Murtipujaka (Deravasi) worship idols.

items.title: For Mains — Jainism
items.body:
## How Mains frames Jainism

Mains (Paper-II, clause M2-1) asks you to *evaluate* Jainism as a social and intellectual movement, not merely to list Tirthankaras. The strongest answers connect its **ethical philosophy** to **social change, art, and contemporary relevance**, and compare it with Buddhism where asked.

| Dimension | Analytical thrust |
|---|---|
| Causes | Reaction to Vedic ritualism, Brahmin monopoly, Kshatriya/Vaishya assertion; use of Prakrit |
| Doctrine | Anekantavada/Syadvada (epistemic pluralism), Ahimsa, Aparigraha, Triratna |
| Social impact | Equality beyond varna, but extreme asceticism limited mass appeal vs Buddhism |
| Culture | Prakrit/Apabhramsha literature; Dilwara, Shravanabelagola, Ellora, Khandagiri art |
| Relevance | Ahimsa → Gandhi; Anekantavada → pluralism/tolerance; Aparigraha → sustainability |

**Data points / anchors to quote:** 24 Tirthankaras (Parshvanatha 23rd, c. 8th c. BCE, historical; Mahavira 24th); First Council **Pataliputra c. 300 BCE** (Sthulabhadra); Second Council **Vallabhi 512 CE** (Devardhigani); patrons **Chandragupta Maurya, Kharavela (Hathigumpha), Kakatiya/Ganga rulers**; **Gommateshwara (Bahubali) at Shravanabelagola** (c. 981 CE, Ganga minister Chamundaraya); Gandhi's acknowledged debt to Jain Ahimsa (Raychandbhai Mehta).

**AP angle:** Jainism had a strong early footprint in Andhra — rock-cut beds and relics at **Guntupalli, Penikalapadu, Danavulapadu, Kolanupaka (Telangana)** and the Jain basadis of the **Rashtrakuta/Eastern Chalukya** era — before Veerashaivism and Vaishnava Bhakti displaced it. A line on this earns the AP-specific mark.

**Use in answers:**
- *Thesis line:* "Jainism's radicalism was ethical, not institutional — its uncompromising Ahimsa won moral authority but its severe asceticism capped its mass spread."
- *Diagram idea:* Triratna triangle (Right Faith–Knowledge–Conduct) → Moksha.
- *Quote:* Mahatma Gandhi on Ahimsa and Anekantavada as the basis of tolerance.
- *Comparison hook:* note that Buddhism's Middle Path spread faster than Jainism's severe asceticism, yet Jainism survived better in India through strong mercantile (Baniya) patronage and institutional continuity.
- *Economic point:* Aparigraha and the restriction on agriculture (which risks harming life) channelled Jains into trade and finance, explaining their lasting commercial prominence in Gujarat, Rajasthan and the Deccan.
- Conclude with contemporary relevance: non-violence, ecological restraint (Aparigraha), and pluralism.
keyPoints: Evaluate Jainism as a social-intellectual movement, not a Tirthankara list.
Link Anekantavada/Syadvada to pluralism and Ahimsa/Aparigraha to Gandhi and sustainability.
Contrast with Buddhism: extreme asceticism limited Jainism's mass appeal.
Cite art/culture: Shravanabelagola Bahubali, Dilwara, Ellora, Prakrit literature.
AP angle: early Jain sites at Guntupalli, Danavulapadu, Kolanupaka before Bhakti displacement.
items.source: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past; A.L. Basham, The Wonder That Was India; NCERT Ancient India
